title: Stable X-ray reverberation lags in the black hole X-ray binary Swift J1727.8-1613
summary: Aims. We investigate the evolution of X-ray reverberation lags in the black hole X-ray binary Swift J1727.8-1613 during its 2023 outburst, with the aim of probing the inner accretion flow geometry across spectral states. Methods. We analyzed NICER observations covering the low-hard state (LHS) and hard-intermediate state (HIMS). The time lags were computed using Fourier-based techniques, and we constructed lag-frequency and lag-energy spectra. To obtain a robust estimate of the soft lag amplitude, we focused on a frequency range in which the reverberation signal dominates and remains stable, thereby minimizing contamination from hard lags and phase-wrapping effects. Results. The soft lag amplitude increases rapidly from the LHS to the early HIMS and then stays near 10 ms throughout the HIMS. In the frequency range in which reverberation lags prevail, the lag shows little dependence on Fourier frequency. On the other hand, the observed low-frequency lags change from hard-lag dominated to soft-lag dominated, with amplitudes comparable to those measured at higher frequencies. Conclusions. These results suggest that the reverberation lag varies little during the HIMS, consistent with a relatively stable inner accretion geometry during this state. The apparent evolution of the lag amplitude from the LHS to the HIMS can be largely explained by the diminishing effect of hard lags and does not necessarily require significant changes in the intrinsic light-travel timescale. Swift J1727.8-1613 therefore provides a case in which the reverberation signal can be studied with reduced contamination over a broad frequency range, offering new insight into the evolution of the accretion geometry in black hole X-ray binaries.

AI.tldr: This paper studies X-ray reverberation lags in the black hole X-ray binary Swift J1727.8-1613 during its 2023 outburst using NICER observations. It finds that soft lag amplitude increases from low-hard to hard-intermediate state and then stabilizes, with the evolution largely explained by diminishing hard lag contamination rather than intrinsic geometry changes.
AI.motivation: To probe the inner accretion flow geometry across spectral states in a black hole X-ray binary by investigating the evolution of X-ray reverberation lags.
AI.method: NICER observations covering the low-hard state (LHS) and hard-intermediate state (HIMS) were analyzed using Fourier-based techniques to compute time lags and construct lag-frequency and lag-energy spectra. A frequency range where reverberation signal dominates was isolated to minimize contamination from hard lags and phase-wrapping effects.
AI.result: Soft lag amplitude increases rapidly from LHS to early HIMS, then stabilizes near 10 ms throughout HIMS. Reverberation-dominated lags show little dependence on Fourier frequency. Low-frequency lags transition from hard-lag dominated to soft-lag dominated.
AI.conclusion: The reverberation lag remains stable during HIMS, suggesting a relatively stable inner accretion geometry. The apparent evolution from LHS to HIMS is largely due to diminishing hard lags, not intrinsic light-travel time changes. This provides a clean case for studying reverberation over a broad frequency range.

title: Gas-Phase Metallicity and Nitrogen Abundances in Low-Mass Galaxies Down to $M_\star\simeq10^{5.7}\,M_\odot$ at $z\simeq4.5$--$10.1$ from JWST Lensing Cluster Surveys
comment: 35 pages, submitted to the Astrophysical Journal
summary: We analyze 405 deep JWST/NIRSpec spectra of star-forming galaxies at $z=4.5$--$10.1$ from DREAMS and other lensing-cluster surveys to study chemical enrichment in intrinsically faint, low-mass galaxies. The sample covers $M_{\rm UV}\simeq-12$ to $-22$ and reaches $M_\star\simeq10^{5.7}\,M_\odot$, with 50\% of the sources at $M_{\rm UV}>-17.5$ magnified by $μ>3$. From individual spectra and mass-binned stacks, we derive the gas-phase metallicity together with nitrogen and carbon abundances using the rest-frame UV and optical lines. \Add{We derive new empirical strong-line metallicity calibrations using direct-method measurements from stellar-mass-binned stacks, reaching a representative stellar mass of $M_\star\simeq10^{6.6}\,M_\odot$. Applying these calibrations, we trace the $z\sim6$ mass--metallicity relation down to $M_\star\simeq10^{6.6}\,M_\odot$, where it reaches $12+\log({\rm O/H})\simeq7.2$, with a low-mass slope slightly steeper than the local relation and in broad agreement with hydrodynamical simulations.} In the $M_\star\simeq10^{7.7}\,M_\odot$ stack, N/O from N\,{\sc iv}]\,$λλ\,1483,1486$ exceeds that from [N\,{\sc ii}]\,$\lambda6583$ by $\simeq1.4$ dex. The UV--optical difference could indicate a localized, highly ionized N-rich component whose high N/O and subsolar C/O resemble nitrogen-rich globular-cluster populations with $M_\star\lesssim10^6\,M_\odot$. \Add{The combination of these abundance patterns and a He\,{\sc ii}\,\W4686/H$β$ ratio of $\simeq0.03$, well above BPASS predictions, suggests that WR stars may contribute both prompt CNO-cycle enrichment and hard ionizing radiation, with the inferred WR population potentially supplying enough nitrogen to account for the excess on globular-cluster scales.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes 405 JWST/NIRSpec spectra of star-forming galaxies at z=4.5–10.1 to study chemical enrichment in low-mass galaxies, deriving new metallicity calibrations down to M⋆~10^6.6 M⊙, tracing the mass–metallicity relation to low masses, and finding evidence for nitrogen-rich populations possibly linked to Wolf–Rayet stars and globular-cluster-like enrichment.
AI.motivation: To understand chemical enrichment in intrinsically faint, low-mass galaxies at high redshift (z=4.5–10.1), probing the mass–metallicity relation and abundance patterns in the early Universe, particularly for galaxies too faint to be studied without JWST and gravitational lensing.
AI.method: Analysis of 405 deep JWST/NIRSpec spectra from DREAMS and lensing-cluster surveys; derivation of gas-phase metallicity, nitrogen, and carbon abundances from rest-frame UV and optical lines; development of new strong-line metallicity calibrations using direct-method measurements from stellar-mass-binned stacks; comparison with BPASS predictions and hydrodynamical simulations.
AI.result: Traced the z~6 mass–metallicity relation down to M⋆~10^6.6 M⊙ with metallicity 12+log(O/H)~7.2; found N/O from NIV] exceeds that from [NII] by ~1.4 dex in M⋆~10^7.7 M⊙ stack; detected HeII λ4686/Hβ~0.03 above BPASS predictions; UV–optical abundance differences suggest N-rich, subsolar C/O populations resembling globular-cluster stars.
AI.conclusion: WR stars may contribute both prompt CNO-cycle enrichment and hard ionizing radiation in low-mass high-z galaxies, potentially supplying enough nitrogen to account for excess on globular-cluster scales.

title: A cosmic-ray loaded nascent outflow driven by a massive star cluster
comment: Published by Nature Communications
summary: Cosmic rays are widely held to drive outflows from star-forming galaxies and profoundly influence galaxy evolution. Direct evidence for cosmic-ray carrying outflows is however lacking. At the same time there is increasing awareness of the importance of massive star clusters in the acceleration of cosmic rays in galaxies. Here we report on the discovery of a nascent outflow driven by the massive star cluster Westerlund 1. Giga-electronvolt gamma-ray emission coincident with a cavity visible in atomic hydrogen traces the emergence of a population of relativistic electrons out of the Galactic Disc. The emission is offset from tera-electronvolt gamma-ray radiation surrounding the cluster, but connects to it smoothly spectrally and spatially. The implied energy density of co-accelerated protons and nuclei, assuming standard non-thermal electron/proton injection efficiencies, is at least an order of magnitude higher than that in the general interstellar medium. These particles therefore have the potential to dynamically influence the outflow. This discovery suggests that cosmic-ray loaded outflows may be a common feature of young massive star clusters, with implications for the transport of cosmic rays into the halo of the Galaxy.

AI.tldr: Discovery of a cosmic-ray driven outflow from the massive star cluster Westerlund 1, evidenced by gamma-ray emission coincident with an atomic hydrogen cavity, suggesting such outflows may be common in young massive star clusters.
AI.motivation: Cosmic rays are theorized to drive outflows from star-forming galaxies and influence galaxy evolution, but direct evidence for cosmic-ray carrying outflows has been lacking. Additionally, the role of massive star clusters in accelerating cosmic rays is increasingly recognized.
AI.method: Observation of GeV gamma-ray emission coincident with an atomic hydrogen cavity near Westerlund 1, analyzed spatially and spectrally in connection with TeV gamma-ray emission from the cluster.
AI.result: The gamma-ray emission offset from TeV radiation but smoothly connected spectrally and spatially; implied energy density of co-accelerated protons and nuclei is at least an order of magnitude higher than the general interstellar medium.
AI.conclusion: Cosmic-ray loaded outflows may be a common feature of young massive star clusters, with implications for cosmic ray transport into the Galactic halo.

title: 22 Newly Identified Repeating Changing-look AGNs and Evidence for Extreme Broad-line Region Breathing
comment: 22 pages, 11 figures, 2 tables, submitted to ApJ
summary: Changing-look active galactic nuclei (CL AGNs) show the appearance or disappearance of broad emission lines on timescales of years. Among them, the repeating CL (RCL) AGNs may provide a clear clue for our understanding of the CL transitions because the same nucleus crosses some physical boundaries more than once. We search for RCL AGNs in known CL-AGN samples using long-term multi-band light curves, and selected 34 candidates for spectroscopic follow-up. We confirm 25 RCL AGNs, including 22 newly identified cases. Properties of these RCL AGNs are analyzed. The observed rest-frame intervals of the second transitions are mostly 3--4 yr, while the variations of the optical light curves suggest that some transitions might occur on timescales of several months. The latest spectra show that the on/off states correspond to higher/lower Eddington-ratio, in the expected direction relative to the parent CL-AGN samples. As seven RCL AGNs are well covered by nearly continuous single-band light curves, their on/off states can be found to follow multi-year optical excursions, and their Eddington ratios vary consistently with the photometric changes. We also find that the H$β$-only transitions occur at higher Eddington ratios than the transitions involving both H$α$ and H$β$, suggesting a line-dependent Broad-Line-Region (BLR) visibility threshold. These results support a picture in which different accretion-flow processes drive reversible changes in the central ionizing emissions, while the observed RCL transitions are produced by the BLR breathing across line-dependent visibility thresholds.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies and characterizes 25 repeating changing-look active galactic nuclei (RCL AGNs), 22 of which are newly discovered. These objects show recurrent appearances/disappearances of broad emission lines. The study finds transition intervals of 3–4 years, line-dependent Eddington-ratio thresholds (Hβ-only transitions occur at higher Eddington ratios than Hα+Hβ transitions), and consistency between photometric variability and on/off states. Results support a model where accretion-flow changes drive reversible ionizing emission variations, and BLR "breathing" across visibility thresholds produces observed RCL transitions.
AI.motivation: Repeating CL AGNs (RCL AGNs) are particularly valuable because they cross the same physical boundaries multiple times, offering clearer insights into the mechanisms behind CL transitions than single-occurrence events.
AI.method: Long-term multi-band light curves were used to search for RCL AGN candidates from known CL-AGN samples. 34 candidates were selected, and 25 were confirmed via spectroscopic follow-up (22 new). Eddington ratios, transition timescales, and line behaviors (Hβ-only vs. Hα+Hβ) were analyzed.
AI.result: 25 RCL AGNs confirmed; rest-frame second transitions mostly 3–4 yr, some optical variations on months. On/off states correspond to higher/lower Eddington ratios; seven with good light-curve coverage show multi-year optical excursions matching Eddington-ratio changes. Hβ-only transitions occur at higher Eddington ratios than those involving both Hα and Hβ.
AI.conclusion: Reversible accretion-flow changes drive variations in central ionizing emissions, and BLR breathing across line-dependent visibility thresholds produces the observed RCL transitions. The line-dependent thresholds (Hβ vs. Hα+Hβ) support a picture of distinct BLR region responses to changing ionizing flux.

title: Non-thermal emission from the vicinity of the magnetar CXOU J171405.7-381031
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: Magnetars are neutron stars with ultra-strong magnetic fields ($B \sim 10^{14}$-$10^{15}$ G) and are promising candidates for high-energy particle acceleration. We present a multiwavelength analysis of the region surrounding CXOU J171405.7-381031, a magnetar associated with the supernova remnant (SNR) CTB 37B. The broadband spectral energy distribution spanning radio to TeV energies is modeled using leptonic and lepto-hadronic scenarios, with particle populations constrained using Markov Chain Monte Carlo techniques. Within an SNR framework, both scenarios provide acceptable descriptions of the gamma-ray data. The purely leptonic model reproduces the overall spectral shape but slightly underestimates the highest-energy flux measured by H.E.S.S., whereas a lepto-hadronic interpretation offers an improved description above $\sim 10$ TeV, with inverse-Compton scattering dominating the GeV emission and neutral-pion decay contributing at the highest energies. The required proton energy ($W_{\rm p} \gtrsim 10^{51}$ erg) can be substantially reduced if the remnant interacts with a dense ambient medium. A magnetar wind nebula scenario can reproduce the broadband spectrum but is strongly disfavored by the observed source morphology. Simulated Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO) observations indicate that exposures of $\sim 50$ h will constrain the proton cut-off energy, enabling a decisive test of hadronic emission in this region.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a multiwavelength analysis of the magnetar CXOU J171405.7-381031 in SNR CTB 37B, modeling its broadband spectrum with leptonic and lepto-hadronic scenarios. The lepto-hadronic model better explains TeV emission via neutral-pion decay, and future CTAO observations can decisively test hadronic components.
AI.motivation: Magnetars are extreme neutron stars with ultra-strong magnetic fields and are promising candidates for high-energy particle acceleration. Understanding their emission mechanisms requires multiwavelength modeling.
AI.method: Multiwavelength spectral energy distribution modeling from radio to TeV using leptonic and lepto-hadronic scenarios, with particle populations constrained via Markov Chain Monte Carlo techniques.
AI.result: Both scenarios describe gamma-ray data acceptably. The leptonic model slightly underestimates H.E.S.S. highest-energy flux; the lepto-hadronic model improves description above ~10 TeV via neutral-pion decay. Required proton energy can be reduced if SNR interacts with dense medium. Magnetar wind nebula scenario is disfavored by morphology.
AI.conclusion: Future CTAO observations (~50 h) can constrain the proton cut-off energy, enabling a decisive test of hadronic emission in this region.

title: The FAST HI 21-cm Absorption Blind Survey. III. OH Absorption Search in the 21-cm Absorber Sample and Continued HI Absorption Search
comment: 20 pages, 15 figures
summary: We present the first blind search for OH 18-cm absorption with the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope (FAST), conducted alongside the HI 21-cm absorption search. Our previous FAST blind HI absorption search identified 34 systems. In this work, we extend the search using 2024 and part of the 2025 CRAFTS and FASHI data (394.4 hr and 1622.1 deg$^{2}$) together with FATHOMER observations, yielding three known and four new HI absorbers, for a total of 41 HI absorption systems. We search for OH absorption in 19 HI absorption systems whose OH redshifted frequencies fall within the FAST band. The known OH absorber towards PKS 1413+135 was re-detected, making our survey the first blind survey to detect OH absorption. No new OH absorbers were identified. We examine the relationship between $N_{\rm{OH}}$ and $N_{\rm{HI}}$, applying survival analysis to account for upper limits. The analysis does not provide statistically significant evidence for either an $N_{\rm{OH}}$-$N_{\rm{HI}}$ correlation or redshift evolution of $N_{\rm{OH}}$/$N_{\rm{HI}}$. Finally, spectral stacking sets 3$σ$ OH column density upper limits of 4.93, 1.64, and 1.72 $T_{\rm{ex}}$/$c_{\rm{f,OH}}\times$10$^{12}$cm$^{-2}$K$^{-1}$ for associated, intervening, and combined samples, corresponding to [\rm{OH}]/[\rm{HI}] ratios of $<$1.66$\times$10$^{-8}$, $<$1.42$\times$10$^{-8}$, and $<$0.90$\times$10$^{-8}$, assuming $T_{\rm{ex}}$=10K for OH and $T_{\rm{s}}$=100K for HI. These results place the strongest constraints to date on the OH content in radio-selected HI absorbers and establish a blind-survey benchmark for future studies of molecular gas in HI-selected systems. They also demonstrate that known HI 21-cm absorbers provide an effective parent sample for systematic OH absorption searches, paving the way for future larger surveys.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first blind search for OH 18-cm absorption using FAST, conducted alongside HI 21-cm absorption surveys. From 394.4 hours of data covering 1622.1 deg², they identified 41 HI absorption systems (34 from previous work, 7 new). Searching for OH in 19 systems with appropriate redshift, they only re-detected the known OH absorber towards PKS 1413+135. No significant correlation between N_OH and N_HI or redshift evolution was found. Spectral stacking placed the strongest upper limits on OH/HI ratios (down to <0.90×10⁻⁸), establishing a benchmark for future blind OH surveys.
AI.motivation: To perform the first blind survey for OH 18-cm absorption using FAST, extending previous blind HI 21-cm absorption searches to probe molecular gas content in HI-selected systems and establish constraints on OH abundance and its relation to HI.
AI.method: Analysis of 2024–2025 CRAFTS and FASHI data (394.4 hr, 1622.1 deg²) plus FATHOMER observations to identify HI 21-cm absorbers. A targeted search for OH 18-cm absorption was conducted in 19 systems where OH frequencies fall within FAST's band. Survival analysis accounting for upper limits was used to examine N_OH–N_HI correlation and redshift evolution. Spectral stacking was performed to derive OH column density upper limits.
AI.result: 41 HI absorption systems total (34 previously known + 7 new). Only one OH detection (PKS 1413+135, previously known). No significant N_OH–N_HI correlation or redshift evolution. Stacking yielded 3σ OH column density upper limits of 4.93, 1.64, and 1.72 T_ex/c_f,OH ×10¹² cm⁻² K⁻¹ for associated, intervening, and combined samples, corresponding to [OH]/[HI] ratios <1.66×10⁻⁸, <1.42×10⁻⁸, and <0.90×10⁻⁸.
AI.conclusion: Results place the strongest constraints to date on OH content in radio-selected HI absorbers, establish a blind-survey benchmark for future molecular gas studies, and demonstrate that HI 21-cm absorbers serve as an effective parent sample for systematic OH absorption searches.

title: Discovery of $γ$-Ray Pulsations from the Extreme-Spin-Down Millisecond Pulsar PSR J0435+3233
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures
summary: Motivated by the recent discovery of PSR~J0435+3233, a millisecond pulsar with an exceptionally large period derivative of $\dot{P}=4.9\times10^{-17}\ {\rm s\,s^{-1}}$ and a high spin-down luminosity of $\dot{E}=5.89\times10^{37}\ {\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$, we analyze $\sim$17~yr of observations obtained with the \textit{Fermi} Large Area Telescope for the pulsar. We identify the cataloged source 4FGL~J0435.5+3232, located only $0.01^{\circ}$ from the radio timing position, as the $γ$-ray counterpart of PSR~J0435+3233. Using $γ$-ray events collected within the validity interval of the radio timing ephemeris, we detect its $γ$-ray pulsations at a $\sim6.8σ$ confidence level. In this interval, the phase-resolved analysis shows that the pulsed emission is concentrated predominantly within the rotational-phase of $φ\sim0.44$--$0.69$. We also derive its $γ$-ray luminosity of $L_γ=6.26\times10^{32}\ {\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$, assuming a distance of 1.2~kpc and isotropic emission. This luminosity corresponds to an apparent $γ$-ray efficiency of $η_γ\sim1.1\times10^{-5}$, revealing an exceptionally low $γ$-ray output despite the pulsar's young-pulsar-like rotational-energy budget. Our detection establishes PSR~J0435+3233 as a $γ$-ray MSP, and the striking combination of its high spin-down power and low apparent $γ$-ray efficiency provides a new probe of particle acceleration, radiation beaming, and viewing geometry in the magnetospheres of millisecond pulsars with extreme rotational properties.

AI.tldr: Using ~17 years of Fermi-LAT data, we identify PSR J0435+3233 as a γ-ray millisecond pulsar with an extremely low γ-ray efficiency (~1.1×10⁻⁵) despite its exceptionally high spin-down luminosity (5.89×10³⁷ erg/s), providing new insights into MSP magnetospheric physics.
AI.motivation: The recent discovery of PSR J0435+3233, a millisecond pulsar with an unusually large period derivative (4.9×10⁻¹⁷ s/s) and high spin-down luminosity, motivated a search for its γ-ray counterpart to understand its emission properties.
AI.method: Analyzed ~17 years of Fermi-LAT observations, identified the γ-ray source 4FGL J0435.5+3232 as the counterpart (0.01° from radio timing position), and performed phase-resolved analysis using radio timing ephemeris to detect pulsations at ~6.8σ.
AI.result: γ-ray pulsations detected at ~6.8σ confidence, pulsed emission concentrated at rotational phase φ~0.44–0.69, γ-ray luminosity L_γ=6.26×10³² erg/s, and apparent efficiency η_γ~1.1×10⁻⁵ — exceptionally low despite the high spin-down power.
AI.conclusion: PSR J0435+3233 is confirmed as a γ-ray MSP; its extreme combination of high spin-down power and low γ-ray efficiency offers a new probe of particle acceleration, radiation beaming, and viewing geometry in millisecond pulsar magnetospheres.

title: Identifying and Distinguishing Quenching Galaxies with Spatially Resolved Star Formation in Mock CASTOR and NGRST Observations
comment: 23 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to OJAp
summary: We present synthetic images of galaxies that are in the stages of star formation quenching for the Cosmological Advanced Survey Telescope for Optical and UV Research (CASTOR) and Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope (NGRST), based on simulations coming from the IllustrisTNG suite, as processed using the stellar population synthesis library \textsc{galaxev}. We account for the effects of dust and various sources of noise to produce mock observations that should mirror real observations. Using these synthetic images, we fit photometric observations in binned circular annuli using \texttt{FAST++} and a flexible star formation history, and recover well the spatially resolved stellar mass and star formation rate. We thereby measure various indicators (morphological metrics) of spatially resolved star formation activity in the context of galaxy quenching. We find that we are able to distinguish quenching galaxies from a mass-matched control sample of normal star forming galaxies. We additionally find that we can distinguish various quenching mechanisms, where galaxies consistent with an inside-out quenching signature can be separated from galaxies that display an outside-in signature. Using machine learning techniques the accuracy of this classification is reliable, and the progress through the quenching episode can be estimated for the different populations of quenching galaxies. We make predictions for the abundance of the various quenching populations in proposed surveys for CASTOR and NGRST, and find that these surveys will enable the classifications of thousands of quenching galaxies out to intermediate redshifts, and more when considering higher redshifts.

AI.tldr: This paper uses synthetic galaxy images from IllustrisTNG simulations to predict how CASTOR and NGRST surveys will observe star formation quenching. They generate mock observations accounting for dust and noise, recover stellar mass and SFR via photometric fitting, and classify quenching galaxies (inside-out vs. outside-in) using morphological metrics and machine learning. They forecast thousands of quenching galaxies detectable out to intermediate and higher redshifts.
AI.motivation: To predict and enable the classification of star formation quenching mechanisms using upcoming CASTOR and NGRST surveys, by testing whether synthetic observations can recover spatially resolved quenching signatures.
AI.method: Simulations from IllustrisTNG processed with GALAXEV stellar population synthesis; dust and noise added to create mock CASTOR/NGRST observations; photometric fitting with FAST++ using flexible star formation histories in binned circular annuli; morphological metrics measured; machine learning used to classify quenching mechanisms (inside-out vs. outside-in).
AI.result: Quenching galaxies can be distinguished from mass-matched normal star-forming galaxies. Inside-out and outside-in quenching signatures can be separated with reliable accuracy via machine learning. Surveys are predicted to classify thousands of quenching galaxies out to intermediate redshifts, with more at higher redshifts.
AI.conclusion: Upcoming CASTOR and NGRST surveys will enable robust, spatially resolved classification of galaxy quenching mechanisms and their evolutionary stages, providing large statistical samples for studying galaxy quenching across cosmic time.

title: Impact of eccentricity and higher-modes on neutron star-black hole parameter estimation
summary: Detections of gravitational waves from neutron star-black hole systems provide avenues for studying extreme matter, constraining binary formation channels, and testing the nature of compact objects in strong gravity. Eccentric signatures in the signal further enhance this potential by improving parameter estimation and offering clues about binary formation. Because eccentricity is primarily imprinted during the inspiral phase, it is often weakly constrained or missed entirely in binary black hole observations; in contrast, neutron star-black hole systems produce longer in-band signals, enabling more precise measurements of eccentricity and leaving a distinct imprint on parameter inference. In this work, we present a systematic parameter-estimation study exploring the impact of eccentricity on inference using injections simulated with the state-of-the-art eccentric waveform model SEOBNRv5EHM. We find that for systems like GW200105_162426, the measurement precision of eccentricity and correlated parameters improves as eccentricity increases, yielding tighter constraints at larger eccentricities. For the highest eccentricity considered in this study, $e=0.25$, we recover eccentricity with $1σ$ uncertainty as low as $4\times10^{-4}$. In addition, the constraints on effective spin $χ_\mathrm{eff}$ and mass ratio $q$ improve relative to the quasi-circular case by factors of $\sim13$ and $\sim20$, respectively. On the other hand, we find no significant improvement in extrinsic parameters such as luminosity distance and sky localization, suggesting that for systems like GW200105_162426, the additional information provided by eccentricity in this sector is either negligible or degenerate with the information provided by higher-order modes.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the impact of eccentricity on parameter estimation for neutron star-black hole (NSBH) gravitational wave signals. Using the SEOBNRv5EHM waveform model, the authors find that higher eccentricity significantly improves measurement precision for eccentricity itself, effective spin (χ_eff), and mass ratio (q), but shows no notable improvement for extrinsic parameters like luminosity distance and sky localization.
AI.motivation: Eccentricity in gravitational wave signals provides valuable information about binary formation and can improve parameter estimation, but its impact is not well-studied for neutron star-black hole (NSBH) systems, which produce longer in-band signals than binary black holes and may enable more precise eccentricity measurements.
AI.method: Systematic parameter-estimation study using injections simulated with the eccentric waveform model SEOBNRv5EHM, analyzing systems similar to GW200105_162426 across varying eccentricities.
AI.result: At e=0.25, eccentricity is recovered with 1σ uncertainty as low as 4×10⁻⁴. Constraints on χ_eff and mass ratio q improve by factors of ~13 and ~20, respectively, compared to quasi-circular case. No significant improvement is found for luminosity distance and sky localization.
AI.conclusion: Eccentricity in NSBH systems substantially improves inference of intrinsic parameters (eccentricity, spin, mass ratio) but does not significantly enhance extrinsic parameter constraints, likely due to degeneracy with higher-order modes.

title: Testing various assumptions for radiolysis, non-diffusive chemistry, and chemical desorption in cold cores
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: To study interstellar gas and grain chemistry, gas-phase astrochemical models have been developed since the early 1980s and gas-grain models since the 1990s. Each published model includes various assumptions mainly for surface processes. In this paper, we compare recently added mechanisms for grain surface chemistry, namely, non-diffusive chemistry, radiolysis, and chemical desorption. Several formalisms for these processes have been added to our astrochemical model Nautilus, and we tested them, comparing the predicted gas-phase and ice abundances. Our predictions are also compared to gas and ice observed compositions. Our main findings are that radiolysis itself does not influence the results. Non-diffusive chemistry can have an impact on the gas-phase and ice species, but it depends on the adopted formalism. In particular, the one of Shingledecker & Herbst (2018) changes the main reservoirs of the species in the ices, impacting the species in the gas-phase as well. The adopted formalism for chemical desorption can produce differences in the gas-phase by up to a factor of ten. Last, our standard model, without non-diffusive chemistry and with the chemical desorption from Fredon et al. (2021), produces the best results in relation to observed gas-phase abundances, while the ice observed agreement is unchanged. The formalism for some grain surface processes are important even for gas-phase abundances. More experiments are needed to constrain their efficiency, however. For the chemical desorption, each formalism relies on an uncertain parameter, which is the fraction of the energy actually delivered to the products, that can be adjusted to reproduce the experiments.

AI.tldr: This paper compares different formalisms for grain surface chemistry mechanisms (non-diffusive chemistry, radiolysis, and chemical desorption) implemented in the astrochemical model Nautilus, finding that radiolysis has negligible impact, non-diffusive chemistry effects depend on the formalism, chemical desorption can alter gas-phase abundances by up to 10x, and the standard model without non-diffusive chemistry with Fredon et al. (2021) chemical desorption best matches observed gas-phase abundances.
AI.motivation: To systematically compare recently added mechanisms for grain surface chemistry (non-diffusive chemistry, radiolysis, and chemical desorption) and evaluate their impact on astrochemical model predictions of gas-phase and ice abundances.
AI.method: Different formalisms for non-diffusive chemistry, radiolysis, and chemical desorption were implemented in the Nautilus astrochemical model. Predicted gas-phase and ice abundances were compared against each other and against observed compositions.
AI.result: Radiolysis has no significant influence. Non-diffusive chemistry impacts gas and ice species but depends on the formalism; Shingledecker & Herbst (2018) formalism alters main reservoirs in ices. Chemical desorption can cause up to 10-fold differences in gas-phase abundances. The standard model (no non-diffusive chemistry, Fredon et al. 2021 chemical desorption) best matches observed gas-phase abundances.
AI.conclusion: Formalisms for grain surface processes significantly affect even gas-phase predictions. More experiments are needed to constrain process efficiencies, particularly the uncertain energy fraction parameter in chemical desorption formalisms.

title: Eccentricity as a Magnifying Glass: Precision Population Inference Enabled by Eccentric Neutron Star--Black Hole Mergers
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Comments are welcome
summary: The formation history of compact binary systems remains one of the key open questions in astrophysics. Theoretical studies generally favor isolated binary evolution for neutron star-black hole (NSBH) systems, which tends to produce nearly circular orbits. However, recent analyses of the gravitational-wave event GW200105 indicate that its source has measurable eccentricity, suggesting that alternative formation channels may also contribute. It has been shown that the intrinsic parameters of eccentric NSBH mergers, such as the component masses and spins, are much better measured than circular mergers with LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) observatories. We explore how such eccentricity-enhanced parameter measurements can affect the inference of NSBH formation channels. We find that sharper measurements of the effective spin parameter $χ_{\rm eff}$ increase the fraction of systems for which negative values can be confidently identified, allowing for the clear measurement of a spin-orbit misaligned event every $\sim 2.5$ eccentric NSBH detections for an isotropically distributed population in the fifth LVK observing run (O5). Improved NS mass measurements provide better constraining power for NS mass distributions, potentially revealing structure and tightening the bounds that can be drawn on their upper and lower masses. Similarly, the recovery of a metallicity-dependent BH mass distribution is improved by eccentricity-enhanced measurements. Finally, we show that the proposed population-level eccentricity distribution for dynamical-formation channels can be tested by the end of O5.

AI.tldr: Eccentric NSBH mergers improve parameter measurements, enabling clearer identification of spin-orbit misalignment, tighter constraints on NS mass distributions, and better recovery of BH mass distributions, with dynamical formation channels testable by LVK O5.
AI.motivation: To understand how eccentricity-enhanced parameter measurements of NSBH mergers can improve the inference of their formation channels, since eccentricity may indicate alternative formation pathways beyond standard isolated binary evolution.
AI.method: The authors explore how eccentricity in NSBH mergers improves measurement precision of intrinsic parameters (masses, spins, χeff) and use these enhanced measurements to infer formation channel properties, including spin-orbit misalignment, NS mass distributions, BH mass distributions, and population-level eccentricity distributions.
AI.result: Eccentric NSBH detections allow identification of a spin-orbit misaligned event every ~2.5 detections (O5, isotropic population). Improved NS mass measurements tighten bounds on mass distributions. Metallicity-dependent BH mass recovery is improved. Population-level eccentricity distributions for dynamical formation are testable by end of O5.
AI.conclusion: Eccentricity-enhanced parameter measurements significantly improve the ability to distinguish between NSBH formation channels, particularly for spin-orbit misalignment, NS mass structure, and dynamical formation scenarios.

title: Chemical Evolution of Galaxies: Past, Present and Future
comment: Paper accepted for publication on Astrophysics and Space Science, 2025 Astronomy Prize Awardees Collection
summary: In this paper I will describe the basic principles of chemical evolution of galaxies, its main ingredients and uncertainties. By means of chemical evolution we can perform the so-called galactic archaeology, which consists in reconstructing the history of star formation of galaxies and in particular of the Milky Way, starting from the observed stellar and gas abundances. Galactic archaeology is a powerful tool to predict also the behaviour of galaxies at high redshift. In particular, we adopt the "time-delay model" which is a way of interpreting the [X/Fe] vs. [Fe/H] relations (X is the abundance of a specific chemical element) in terms of different timescales of the stellar progenitors of the chemical elements relative to Fe, which is the indicator of "metallicity". I will then describe how we can reconstruct the star formation histories of galaxies of different morphological type (spirals, ellipticals) starting from the available observations. Particular attention will be paid to the study of the Milky Way which is the best studied galaxy at the moment. I will start describing the first chemical evolution models and then the most recent ones, the main difference between the old and new models being the observational data to compare with. Finally, I will foresee which could be the future improvements to chemical models and what constraints can we derive to better understand galaxy evolution.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews the principles of galactic chemical evolution, using the "time-delay model" to interpret [X/Fe] vs. [Fe/H] relations and reconstruct star formation histories of galaxies (spirals, ellipticals, and especially the Milky Way), tracing the evolution from early models to modern ones and outlining future improvements.
AI.motivation: To describe how chemical evolution models enable galactic archaeology — reconstructing star formation histories from observed stellar and gas abundances — and to highlight the capabilities and uncertainties of this approach for understanding galaxy evolution across cosmic time.
AI.method: Adopts the "time-delay model" which interprets [X/Fe] vs. [Fe/H] relations based on different nucleosynthetic timescales of stellar progenitors relative to Fe; compares model predictions with observed abundances across morphological galaxy types.
AI.result: Shows how star formation histories can be reconstructed for spirals and ellipticals, with particular success for the Milky Way; traces the evolution from early to recent chemical evolution models, where the key difference lies in the improved observational constraints available for comparison.
AI.conclusion: Chemical evolution models are powerful for galactic archaeology and high-redshift galaxy predictions; future improvements will come from better observational constraints and refined model ingredients to further constrain galaxy evolution.

title: X-ray polarization of Z-type neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries -- II. Spectropolarimetric analysis
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables
summary: IXPE has provided for the first time detailed energy- and time-resolved X-ray polarimetry of Z-type neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries (NS-LMXBs) as they move along their color-color diagrams (CCDs). These sources can reach the highest polarization observed for NS-LXMBs in the 2-8 keV range when they move along the horizontal branch. In a previous paper, we characterized the spectral state of a sample of Z-sources using the CCD and estimated the polarization with model-independent analysis. Here, we present detailed spectropolarimetric analysis for each source on each branch using data from IXPE, NICER, and NuSTAR. The continuum X-ray emission of all the sources is well described with a combination of thermal accretion disk emission plus a harder Comptonized component. In addition, reflection features, in particular the relativistically broadened Fe line, are observed for our sources, except GX 5-1. For most of the sources and branches, the main contribution to the X-ray emission and polarization is due to Comptonization: moving from the horizontal branch (HB) to the normal branch (NB), the polarization degree (PD) in the 2-8 keV band varies from about 6% to 3-4%, while the PD is loosely constrained in the flaring branch (FB), due to the shorter exposures. These PD values are significantly higher than theoretical expectations for typical spreading or boundary layer configurations. The polarization of the disk is generally lower (below 3%) but still higher than predictions for an electron scattering-dominated, plane-parallel atmosphere above the disk observed at the corresponding inclination. Moreover, the polarization angle (PA) of the disk seems to be significantly misaligned and not perpendicular to that of Comptonization. We find no correlation between the polarization signal and the inclination, nor with the contribution of reflected photons throughout the Z-track.

AI.tldr: This paper presents detailed spectropolarimetric analysis of Z-type neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries using IXPE, NICER, and NuSTAR data. The study finds that Comptonization dominates X-ray emission and polarization, with polarization degree varying from ~6% on the horizontal branch to 3-4% on the normal branch. Disk polarization is lower (<3%) but higher than theoretical predictions, and polarization angles between disk and Comptonization are misaligned.
AI.motivation: To characterize the spectral states and polarization properties of Z-type NS-LMXBs across their color-color diagrams, building on previous model-independent analysis, and to understand the physical mechanisms driving X-ray emission and polarization in these systems.
AI.method: Spectropolarimetric analysis combining data from IXPE (polarimetry), NICER, and NuSTAR (spectroscopy) for each source on each branch (horizontal, normal, flaring). Continuum modeled with thermal accretion disk emission plus a harder Comptonized component, with reflection features (relativistically broadened Fe line) included for most sources.
AI.result: Comptonization dominates X-ray emission and polarization. PD varies from ~6% (HB) to 3-4% (NB), loosely constrained in FB. Disk PD <3%, higher than theoretical predictions. PA of disk misaligned and not perpendicular to Comptonization PA. No correlation found between polarization and inclination or reflected photon contribution.
AI.conclusion: Observed polarization levels are significantly higher than theoretical expectations for spreading/boundary layer configurations, and disk polarization exceeds predictions for electron scattering-dominated plane-parallel atmospheres. The misalignment between disk and Comptonization polarization angles suggests complex geometry in these systems.

title: The S-PLUS Fifth Data-Release: Over 4500 square degrees of the Southern Sky and a multicolor view of the Hydra and Antlia galaxy clusters
comment: 18 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to ApJ and revised
summary: We present the 5th data release (DR5) of the Southern Photometric Local Universe Survey (S-PLUS), covering 4592 square degrees across 2491 fields. Observations were conducted with the T80-South, a Brazilian robotic telescope equipped with the Javalambre 12-filter system, containing five broad- and seven narrowband filters. Data products feature FITS images and extensive catalogs containing fluxes, magnitudes, and shape parameters for over 113 million detections. In addition, several value-added catalogs are provided, offering photometric redshifts (photo-zs), object classifications, masks, and extinction coefficients. For the first time, this release includes coverage of 110 square degrees along the Galactic disk, facilitating new research into Galactic structure and stellar populations. The release also provides full coverage of the Hydra Supercluster and numerous other nearby clusters with improved data reduction and calibration, enhancing photo-z accuracy, which is vital for large-scale structure studies. A preliminary analysis of the Hydra and Antlia galaxy clusters up to $5 \times R_{200}$ yields an updated catalog of 1706 cluster members based on both spectroscopic and high-quality photo-zs. Our photometric data shows that both clusters have a similar proportion of galaxies with an H$α$ excess relative to their clustercentric distance, though Hydra has a higher fraction near its center. Additionally, the spatial distribution of all objects in our sample highlights a bridge connecting both clusters. We verify that S-PLUS DR5 provides a solid foundation for future scientific investigations, ranging from Solar System studies to Cosmology.

AI.tldr: S-PLUS DR5 covers 4592 sq deg with 113M+ detections using a 12-filter system, including new Galactic disk coverage, improved photo-zs, and a catalog of 1706 cluster members in Hydra and Antlia, with evidence of a bridge connecting both clusters.
AI.motivation: To release the 5th data release of S-PLUS, expanding sky coverage (including the Galactic disk for the first time), improving data reduction and calibration, and providing value-added catalogs (photo-zs, classifications, masks) to enable studies from Solar System science to cosmology and large-scale structure.
AI.method: Observations with the T80-South robotic telescope using the Javalambre 12-filter system (5 broad + 7 narrow). Data products: FITS images, catalogs of fluxes/magnitudes/shapes for 113M+ detections, value-added catalogs with photo-zs, classifications, masks, extinction. Hydra/Antlia cluster analysis using spectroscopic and high-quality photo-zs up to 5×R200.
AI.result: 4592 sq deg across 2491 fields; 113M+ detections; first 110 sq deg along the Galactic disk; full coverage of Hydra Supercluster; updated catalog of 1706 cluster members in Hydra and Antlia; both clusters have similar Hα excess proportion vs. clustercentric distance, but Hydra has higher fraction near center; a spatial bridge connecting both clusters is detected.
AI.conclusion: S-PLUS DR5 provides a solid foundation for future scientific investigations ranging from Solar System studies to cosmology.

title: Radio-detected Lya emitters at 1.88 < z < 3.52: AGN fraction and Lya emission
comment: 14 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics (A&A)
summary: Lya emitters (LAEs) are galaxies with strong Lya emission, tracing early star formation and ionizing radiation. Their connection to active galactic nuclei (AGNs) is key to understanding the mechanisms behind (extended) Lya emission. In this work, we measure the fraction of LAEs identified as radio-emitting AGN (fAGN,radio) and the fraction of radio sources that exhibit Lya emission (fLya) to investigate the connection between radio AGN activity and Lya emission at 1.88 < z < 3.52. We identify 928 sources detected in both the Hobby-Eberly Telescope Dark Energy Experiment (HETDEX) and the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR) surveys. These matches are drawn from 55,109 spectroscopically confirmed LAEs and 27,625 radio sources. After applying completeness corrections, we obtain fAGN,radio = 1.77 $\pm$ 0.04% and fLya = 18.15 $\pm$ 0.14%. The fraction fAGN,radio increases from 0.4 $\pm$ 0.1% to 9.7 $\pm$ 1.3% with increasing Lya luminosity, while fLya rises from 0.7 $\pm$ 0.1% to 55.8 $\pm$ 14.5% with radio luminosity. `LAEs with radio AGN' and `optical AGN with Lya emission' show similar radio luminosities above the AGN threshold, although optical AGN have higher Lya luminosities. We find no significant correlation between Lya luminosity and either radio luminosity or spectral index. Lya line width increases with Lya luminosity but shows no correlation with radio size. Our results show that most Lya emission at 1.88 < z < 3.52 is powered by star formation, with radio AGN activity confined to a small luminous subset (1.77 $\pm$ 0.04%). The absence of correlations between Lya and radio properties suggests that Lya emission is governed primarily by host-galaxy gas properties rather than direct AGN jet coupling.

AI.tldr: The study measures the fraction of Lya emitters (LAEs) that are radio-emitting AGN (1.77%) and the fraction of radio sources showing Lya emission (18.15%) at z~1.88–3.52 using HETDEX and LOFAR data. Both fractions increase with luminosity. No significant correlation is found between Lya and radio properties, suggesting Lya emission is primarily powered by star formation rather than direct AGN jet coupling.
AI.motivation: To understand the connection between radio AGN activity and Lya emission in galaxies at high redshift (1.88 < z < 3.52), specifically whether AGN jets significantly power or influence extended Lya emission.
AI.method: Cross-matched 55,109 HETDEX LAEs with 27,625 LOFAR radio sources to obtain 928 matched sources. Applied completeness corrections and measured fractions fAGN,radio (LAEs identified as radio AGN) and fLya (radio sources with Lya emission) as functions of luminosity.
AI.result: fAGN,radio = 1.77±0.04%, fLya = 18.15±0.14%. fAGN,radio increases from 0.4% to 9.7% with Lya luminosity; fLya rises from 0.7% to 55.8% with radio luminosity. No significant correlation between Lya luminosity and radio luminosity or spectral index. Lya line width correlates with Lya luminosity but not radio size.
AI.conclusion: Most Lya emission at z~1.88–3.52 is powered by star formation. Radio AGN activity is confined to a small, luminous subset (~1.8%). The lack of correlations between Lya and radio properties indicates Lya emission is governed primarily by host-galaxy gas properties, not direct AGN jet coupling.

title: Infrared spectroscopy of gas-phase hydrogenated and methylated pyrenes: from laboratory spectra to the simulated 3.4 $μ$m emission band
comment: 19 pages, 21 figures
summary: Observations of the aromatic infrared emission band at 3.3 $μ$m often reveal satellite emission features in the 3.4 - 3.6 $μ$m range. While the 3.3 $μ$m band is attributed to the CH stretching vibration of polycylic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), the satellite bands - particularly its prominent 3.4 $μ$m component - is assigned to aliphatic CH stretching vibrations in hydrogenated and methylated PAH-like species. Our aim is to derive state-of-the-art infrared emission spectra for aliphatic-containing pyrene derivatives and compare them with astronomical observations. This will help refine our understanding of the contribution of these species to the 3.4 $μ$m emission band. Mid-infrared spectra (1.4-25 $μ$m) of gas-phase dihydropyrene, tehtrahydropyrene, hexahydropyrene methylated pyrene, and pyrene were recorded at temperatures ranging from 373 to 673 K, depending on the species. The band profiles were analyzed using a multi-component fitting tool, and empirical anharmonicity laws were derived to quantify the evolution of the band positions and widths with temperature. The obtained spectral data was combined with the results of a Monte Carlo emission model to simulate the emission spectra following UV-photon absorption, up to the dissociation limit ($\lesssim$6 eV). The resulting synthetic spectra were compared with James Webb Space Telescope observations of the Orion Bar region (PDRs4All program). Based on these state-of-the-art simulated spectra, we propose 1,2,3,6,7,8-hexahydropyrene as the carrier of the red component of the 3.4 $μ$m band observed at 3.403 $μ$m. While 1-methylpyrene may also contribute to the underlying emission plateau, its lack of a strong infrared band complicates detection in observed spectra, unlike hexahydropyrene. All experimental spectra and their temperature-dependent analyses are available in the new cosmicPAH-IRDB database.

AI.tldr: The study investigates aliphatic-containing pyrene derivatives as carriers of the 3.4 μm emission band observed in space, identifying 1,2,3,6,7,8-hexahydropyrene as the primary contributor to the red component at 3.403 μm, using gas-phase IR spectra (373-673 K), empirical anharmonicity laws, Monte Carlo emission modeling, and comparisons with JWST Orion Bar observations.
AI.motivation: To refine the understanding of the contribution of aliphatic-containing PAH-like species to the 3.4 μm satellite emission band observed alongside the aromatic 3.3 μm PAH band in astronomical spectra.
AI.method: Mid-infrared spectra of gas-phase pyrene derivatives (dihydropyrene, tetrahydropyrene, hexahydropyrene, methylated pyrene, pyrene) were recorded at 373-673 K, analyzed with multi-component fitting, and empirical anharmonicity laws derived for temperature-dependent band evolution. These data were combined with Monte Carlo emission modeling to simulate spectra after UV absorption up to ~6 eV, then compared with JWST Orion Bar observations.
AI.result: 1,2,3,6,7,8-hexahydropyrene is identified as the carrier of the red component of the 3.4 μm band at 3.403 μm. 1-methylpyrene may contribute to the underlying plateau but lacks a strong IR band for clear detection.
AI.conclusion: State-of-the-art simulated spectra from laboratory experiments and modeling provide improved spectral assignments for the 3.4 μm emission feature, with hexahydropyrene as a key carrier. All experimental data are publicly available in the cosmicPAH-IRDB database.

title: Dynamics and geometry of the inner sub-parsec-scale jet in 3C 279 observed with the Event Horizon Telescope
comment: accepted for publication by A&A
summary: The 2021 Event Horizon Telescope observations resolve the innermost jet region of the blazar 3C279 with unprecedented detail. The reconstructed images consistently reveal a compact core elongated nearly orthogonal to the large-scale jet axis. This rarely observed morphology recurs across multiple epochs and from 22-230 GHz and is therefore intrinsic rather than an imaging artifact. Geometric model fitting identifies several components with apparent speeds up to 10c, requiring bulk Lorentz factors greater than 10.3 and constraining viewing angles to extremely small values (smaller than one degree). Rest-frame brightness temperatures are systematically low (between 10^9 and 10^10 K), consistent with optically thin emission at 230 GHz. These results suggest that the jet bends toward the observer on sub-parsec scales, producing strong relativistic beaming. Possible drivers of the observed jet bending and temporal evolution include the jet's interaction with the interstellar medium, kink or Kelvin--Helmholtz instabilities, magnetic reconnection near the horizon, or binary-induced precession. However, the current temporal coverage of VLBI data remains insufficient to distinguish between these mechanisms. Continued multifrequency VLBI monitoring will be essential to constraining the dynamics and geometry of the jet base in 3C279.

AI.tldr: EHT 2021 observations of blazar 3C279 reveal a compact core elongated orthogonal to the large-scale jet axis, with apparent superluminal motion up to 10c, Lorentz factors >10.3, and viewing angles <1°, indicating a sub-parsec scale jet bend toward the observer. Low brightness temperatures (~10^9-10^10 K) suggest optically thin 230 GHz emission. Possible bending mechanisms include ISM interaction, instabilities, magnetic reconnection, or binary precession, but current data cannot distinguish them.
AI.motivation: To resolve the innermost jet region of the blazar 3C279 at unprecedented angular resolution using EHT 2021 observations, and to investigate the intrinsic jet morphology, kinematics, and physical conditions at the jet base on sub-parsec scales.
AI.method: Event Horizon Telescope observations at 22-230 GHz across multiple epochs; geometric model fitting of reconstructed images to identify jet components and measure apparent speeds, brightness temperatures, and Lorentz factors.
AI.result: Compact core elongated nearly orthogonal to the large-scale jet axis; components with apparent speeds up to 10c; bulk Lorentz factors >10.3; viewing angles <1°; rest-frame brightness temperatures ~10^9-10^10 K.
AI.conclusion: The jet bends toward the observer on sub-parsec scales, producing strong relativistic beaming. Multiple possible mechanisms exist but cannot be distinguished with current VLBI temporal coverage; continued multifrequency VLBI monitoring is needed.

title: Euclid: Calibrating distances from surface brightness fluctuations with Early Release Observations of the Fornax cluster
comment: 22 pages, 14 figures
summary: Surface brightness fluctuations (SBF), the pixel-to-pixel variations in flux that arise from the statistical distribution of stars in galaxy images, provide a powerful tool to measure redshift-independent distances from photometric data alone. This method is particularly important in the era of large imaging surveys, such as those carried out during the Euclid mission. Here we present the first application of SBF to Euclid data, using the FAST-SBF code to measure stellar fluctuation amplitudes in the $I_\mathrm{E}$ band for a sample of galaxies in the Early Release Observations (ERO) of the Fornax galaxy cluster. Although the Euclid data reduction pipeline is not optimized for SBF measurements, extensive testing suggests that we are able to extract robust results. We calibrate the absolute fluctuation magnitude $\overline{M}_\mathrm{IE}$ as a function of the $(I_\mathrm{E}{-}H_\mathrm{E})$ colour for 15 galaxies in Fornax, then test this relation on galaxies in two other ERO fields: the Perseus cluster and dwarf satellite candidates around NGC 6744. Overall, we find reasonable agreement with distances in the literature and good agreement in cases where FAST-SBF indicates the measurements are robust. Finally, we compare our results against Stellar Population Tools (SPoT) simple stellar population models, and discuss the possibility of using SBF with Euclid to probe the underlying stellar populations of the galaxies.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first application of Surface Brightness Fluctuations (SBF) to Euclid data, using the FAST-SBF code to measure distances to galaxies in the Fornax cluster, Perseus cluster, and NGC 6744 field from Early Release Observations. They calibrate the absolute fluctuation magnitude as a function of color and find reasonable agreement with literature distances, demonstrating the potential of Euclid for SBF-based distance measurement and stellar population studies.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate the feasibility and robustness of measuring SBF-based distances using Euclid imaging data, which is crucial for enabling precise redshift-independent distances from large-scale photometric surveys in the Euclid era.
AI.method: Applied the FAST-SBF code to measure stellar fluctuation amplitudes in the I_E band from Euclid ERO data of the Fornax cluster, Perseus cluster, and NGC 6744 dwarf satellite candidates. Calibrated the absolute fluctuation magnitude M_I_E as a function of (I_E - H_E) color for 15 Fornax galaxies, then tested this calibration on the other fields. Compared results against literature distances and SPoT simple stellar population models.
AI.result: Extracted robust SBF measurements despite Euclid's data reduction pipeline not being optimized for SBF. Found reasonable agreement with literature distances overall, with good agreement when FAST-SBF indicated robust measurements.
AI.conclusion: Euclid data can be used for SBF-based distance measurements, and SBF with Euclid has potential to probe underlying stellar populations of galaxies.

title: Morphologies of SAGAbg low-mass galaxies in Legacy Survey multi-band imaging: dependence on stellar masses, star-formation rates and low-redshift evolution
comment: 24 pages, 16 figures. Submitted to ApJ
summary: The optical morphologies of low-mass galaxies can be used to directly trace their assembly and constrain models of galaxy evolution. We select a sample of 6211 low-mass ($7\lesssim {\rm log}(M_{\ast}/M_{\odot})\lesssim 10$) star-forming galaxies from the SAGAbg catalog that has high-completeness at low-redshifts ($z<0.1$). We obtain their galaxy maps in the $griz$ - bands of the Legacy Surveys and apply STATMORPH to calculate non-parametric morphological measures including the Gini index, $M_{20}$ measure, and CAS parameters. We study how resolution and signal-to-noise affect the morphology measures and find that the bulge strength measurements are the most reliable. The sequence in Gini$-M_{20}$ space is directly linked to the star-forming sequence of galaxies and is dominated by Sb/Sc/Ir morphologies. The $g$-band light distributions are the least concentrated among all the bands. The systematic trends of $M_{20}$ with respect to stellar mass and GALEX NUV-derived specific star formation rate (sSFR) strongly indicate that the galaxies with flatter light profiles are less massive with higher sSFR and vice-versa. We statistically infer that star-forming low-mass galaxies predominantly have disk morphologies with bulges becoming more prominent in quenched systems at higher masses (${\rm log}(M_{\ast}/M_{\odot})\gtrsim 9$).

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the optical morphologies of 6211 low-mass star-forming galaxies (M*/M⊙ ~ 10^7–10^10, z<0.1) from the SAGAbg catalog using Legacy Surveys and STATMORPH. Non-parametric measures (Gini, M20, CAS) reveal that bulge strength is most reliable, g-band light is least concentrated, and flatter profiles correlate with lower mass and higher sSFR. Low-mass star-forming galaxies are predominantly disk-dominated, with bulges emerging in quenched systems above log(M*/M⊙)≳9.
AI.motivation: To use optical morphologies of low-mass galaxies as direct tracers of their assembly history and to constrain galaxy evolution models, leveraging high-completeness low-redshift data.
AI.method: Selected 6211 low-mass star-forming galaxies from SAGAbg (z<0.1), obtained griz-band Legacy Surveys images, computed non-parametric morphological measures (Gini, M20, CAS) via STATMORPH, and analyzed resolution/SNR effects and correlations with stellar mass and sSFR.
AI.result: Bulge strength is the most reliable measure; g-band light is least concentrated; M20 trends with stellar mass and sSFR show flatter profiles in less massive, higher-sSFR galaxies; Gini-M20 sequence links to the star-forming sequence with Sb/Sc/Ir morphologies dominant.
AI.conclusion: Star-forming low-mass galaxies predominantly exhibit disk morphologies, with bulges becoming more prominent in quenched systems at higher masses (log(M*/M⊙)≳9).
